source_refs.note: Topic 5.2, printed pages 128-129: metal ions, prosthetic groups, coenzymes, apoenzyme and holoenzyme, and NAD+.

blocks.text: Many enzymes use additional chemical components to aid in catalysis. These additional non-protein components are cofactors. There are three kinds of cofactor: metal ions, prosthetic groups and coenzymes.

blocks.title: Apoenzyme and holoenzyme
blocks.text: The protein part of an enzyme is the apoenzyme, and the complete enzyme including its cofactor is the holoenzyme.

Many enzymes use metal ions such as Ca2+, Mg2+, Mn2+, Cu2+ and Zn2+ as their cofactors. These metal ions change the non-functional active sites of enzymes into functional sites. The attachment of a cofactor also changes the shape of the enzyme and allows it to combine with its substrate.

blocks.title: Trace elements
blocks.text: Many trace elements such as molybdenum and manganese, which are necessary for our health, are used by enzymes as cofactors.
Some cofactors form covalent bonds with the enzyme and are known as prosthetic groups. A prosthetic group may be an organic compound, for example haematin.

When the cofactor is a non-protein organic molecule loosely attached to the enzyme, it is a coenzyme. Coenzymes take part in enzyme-catalysed reactions, often by transporting electrons (hydrogen atoms) from one enzyme to another. Many vitamins, for example niacin and riboflavin, function as coenzymes, and some are part of coenzymes.

The most important coenzyme in the cell is the hydrogen acceptor nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). When NAD+ acquires a hydrogen atom from an enzyme, it is reduced to NADH. The electron of the hydrogen atom contains energy that the NADH molecule carries. For example, when food is oxidised in the cell, enzymes draw electrons from the food molecules and transfer them to NAD+, which is reduced to NADH.

blocks.caption: The three kinds of cofactor
rows: Make the active site functional; change the enzyme's shape
Ca2+, Mg2+, Mn2+, Cu2+, Zn2+; molybdenum, manganese

blocks.prompt: Zinc is needed by an enzyme to convert its substrate, and NAD+ carries hydrogen away from another. Name the kind of cofactor in each case, and explain the difference between a prosthetic group and a coenzyme.
blocks.explanation: Zinc is a metal ion cofactor; NAD+ is a coenzyme. A prosthetic group is bound to the enzyme by covalent bonds, while a coenzyme is a non-protein organic molecule only loosely attached, which can carry electrons or hydrogen from one enzyme to another.

items: Cofactors are non-protein helpers: apoenzyme (protein) plus cofactor gives the holoenzyme.

Metal ions (Ca2+, Mg2+, Mn2+, Cu2+, Zn2+) make the active site functional; prosthetic groups (haematin) are covalently bound; coenzymes (NAD+, vitamins such as niacin and riboflavin) are loosely attached and carry electrons or hydrogen.
NAD+ accepts a hydrogen atom to become NADH, which carries the energy of that electron, as when food is oxidised.
